title: Case studies: four countries, four populations

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Four required case studies, each written out with place-specific detail: an over-populated country (Bangladesh), an under-populated country (Australia), a country with a high rate of natural population growth (Niger) and a country with a low rate of growth, or decline (Japan). Learn the named places, the rounded figures with their years, and the dates, because place-specific detail is what lifts a case-study answer from a list of general points.

blocks.heading: Over-populated: Bangladesh
blocks.text: Bangladesh, a low-income country on the Ganges delta, had about 170 million people in 2022, most of them packed onto the farmland of that delta where three great rivers meet the sea. Its birth rate was around 18 per 1000 and its death rate around 9 per 1000 in the early 2020s, so the population still grows by roughly 1 per cent a year, and the United Nations expects it to add tens of millions more before it levels off. The pressure shows first in the land: farms average well under a hectare, and each inheritance divides fields too small to feed a family further, so more of the rural poor are pushed onto marginal ground that floods from the rivers or the sea. It shows in services and work as well: city schools run several shifts a day, rural clinics serve far more people than they were built for, and job seekers outnumber formal jobs, keeping pay low. The country has pushed back with family planning: health workers take contraception out to the villages, girls' schooling has risen, and the birth rate has come down from about 34 per 1000 in the 1980s to around 18 by the early 2020s, one of the faster falls in South Asia. Bangladesh shows that over-population is about people against resources, not people alone: the delta is fertile, but the numbers outrun it.

blocks.heading: Under-populated: Australia
blocks.text: Australia is a continent of 7.7 million square kilometres with about 26 million people (2022), an average of around 3 per square kilometre, against roughly 1125 per square kilometre in Bangladesh. Its resources are enormous: iron ore in the Pilbara, coal in Queensland, gas off the north-west coast and vast grazing land across the interior. Yet the interior is desert, so water, not space, decides where people can live, and most of the population clusters in a few coastal cities such as Sydney, Melbourne and Perth. The result is under-population relative to the resources: inland farms, mines and services cannot find workers, so shifts go unfilled and land is left undeveloped, and markets are too thin to support services that a town of ordinary size would keep. Australia deliberately recruits migrants to close the gap: a skilled migration scheme selects the workers the interior and professional services need, so immigration is designed to bring the labour the resources cannot be worked without, and migration, not births, supplies most of the country's population growth. Australia shows the other half of the definition: too few people to use what the land offers, even though the land offers a great deal, and the lesson cuts both ways, because the same country can hold crowded cities and an under-populated interior at once, so a single average density, 3 per square kilometre, hides both conditions at the same time.

blocks.heading: High natural growth: Niger
blocks.text: Niger, in the Sahel south of the Sahara, had around 26 million people in 2022 and one of the world's highest rates of natural increase: a birth rate around 45 per 1000 against a death rate around 9 per 1000 in the early 2020s, growth close to 3.7 per cent a year. At that pace the population doubles in about two decades, which means a country of about 26 million must feed, school and employ around 52 million by the mid-2040s on the same dry farmland along the Niger river and its tributaries. The birth rate stays high because children support their parents on family farms, girls marry young and average only a few years of school, and contraception reaches a small minority of women. The consequences show in age and land: nearly half the population is under 15, so schools and clinics must serve an enormous child cohort with too few teachers and nurses, and harvests fail often in the dry years, as they did for millions of people in 2021-22, when poor rains left households short of food and herders moved south with their cattle in search of grazing. Niger is the high-growth case against Japan in the next section: the two make the contrast the syllabus asks for wherever it names a high-growth and a low-growth country together.

blocks.heading: Low growth and decline: Japan
blocks.text: Japan, an island nation of cities squeezed between mountains and the sea, saw its population peak around 125 million in 2008-10 and fall every year since, to about 124 million by 2023. Its birth rate is near 6-7 per 1000 against a death rate near 12-13 per 1000, so deaths outnumber births year after year and the population shrinks. Births are few because marrying late and having one child, or none, fits the cost of city life, housing and education; few couples have a third child, and a generation raised in that pattern is now the one having, or not having, the next. The results show in ageing: about 29-30 per cent of the population is 65 or over (2023), a shrinking workforce supports the older cohort through national insurance and pensions, and rural services close, as village schools and little-used train lines have done across the mountain valleys, so whole prefectures now hold fewer children than care homes. The government pays pro-natalist benefits and parental leave and allows some immigration, though the intake is small, so policy has slowed rather than reversed the fall, and the population is projected to keep shrinking for decades, below 120 million in the 2040s on national estimates.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: These four countries answer any 7-mark question that asks for a named country: an over-populated one (Bangladesh), an under-populated one (Australia), a high-growth one (Niger) and a declining one (Japan). Niger and Japan are a contrasting pair, as the syllabus asks for where it names high and low growth together: one has nearly half its people under 15, the other nearly a third over 65, and the two patterns ask opposite things of a government, schools and clinics in one case, pensions and care homes in the other. The measures Bangladesh used, family planning taken to villages and schooling for girls, connect back to the population policies in the first half of this topic, and the age groups Niger and Japan carry lead into population structure, topic 1.3. When a 7-mark question names the kind of country, match it to the right case: Bangladesh for over-populated, Australia for under-populated, Niger for high natural growth, Japan for low growth or decline.
